topics.title: Cells
topics.description: Cell structures and how they support life.

lessons.title: Cells: the basic units of life

sections.heading: What is a cell?
sections.body: A cell is the smallest unit that can carry out the processes of life. Some organisms consist of one cell, while plants and animals are made of many specialised cells. Cells contain cytoplasm enclosed by a cell membrane. The membrane controls what enters and leaves the cell.

sections.heading: Structures in plant and animal cells
sections.body: The nucleus contains genetic material and helps control cell activities. Mitochondria release usable energy during respiration. Plant cells also have a cellulose cell wall for support, chloroplasts for photosynthesis in green tissues, and a large permanent vacuole containing cell sap. Animal cells do not have a cellulose cell wall or chloroplasts.

keyTerms.definition: A thin, selectively permeable boundary that controls movement into and out of a cell.
The jelly-like material where many cell reactions take place.
A plant-cell organelle containing chlorophyll, where photosynthesis takes place.

questions.prompt: What is one main function of the cell membrane?
options: It makes food in every cell
It controls what enters and leaves the cell
It stores all the cell's water
questions.explanation: The cell membrane is selectively permeable. It regulates the movement of substances into and out of the cell.

questions.prompt: Which structure contains most of a cell's genetic material?
questions.explanation: The nucleus contains the chromosomes, which carry most of the cell's genetic information.

topics.title: Movement in and out of cells

sections.heading: Diffusion
sections.body: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration, due to their random motion. It does not require the cell to use energy. Oxygen can diffuse into cells when its concentration is higher outside than inside.

sections.heading: Osmosis and active transport
sections.body: Osmosis is the net movement of water molecules through a selectively permeable membrane from a more dilute solution to a more concentrated solution. Active transport moves substances against a concentration gradient and requires energy from respiration. Root cells can use active transport to absorb some mineral ions from the soil.

keyTerms.definition: A difference in the concentration of a substance between two places.
Net movement of water through a selectively permeable membrane from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution.
Movement of substances against a concentration gradient using energy.

questions.prompt: In which direction is the net movement of particles during diffusion?
options: From lower to higher concentration only
questions.explanation: Diffusion produces a net movement down the concentration gradient, from higher concentration to lower concentration.

options: Movement of any particle using energy
Movement of water through a selectively permeable membrane
Movement of water through a cell wall only
Breakdown of glucose in a cell
questions.explanation: Osmosis specifically concerns the net movement of water molecules through a selectively permeable membrane.

topics.title: Plant structure
topics.description: How roots, stems, leaves, and stomata are adapted to their roles.

sections.heading: Roots and stems
sections.body: Roots anchor a plant and absorb water and mineral ions. Root-hair cells have long extensions that increase the surface area available for absorption. Stems support leaves and flowers and contain transport tissues. Xylem carries water and mineral ions mainly from roots towards the rest of the plant; phloem transports dissolved sugars to places where they are needed or stored.

sections.heading: Leaves and gas exchange
sections.body: A leaf is broad and usually thin, helping it capture light and allowing gases to diffuse over short distances. Stomata are pores, often more numerous on the lower leaf surface. Guard cells change shape to open or close each pore, regulating gas exchange and water loss.

keyTerms.definition: A root-cell extension that increases the surface area for absorbing water and mineral ions.
Plant tissue that conducts water and mineral ions.
A pore in a leaf surface controlled by guard cells.

questions.prompt: How does a root-hair cell help a plant?
options: It increases the surface area for absorption
It carries sugars to the roots
questions.explanation: The long extension increases surface area, helping the root absorb water and mineral ions from the soil.

questions.prompt: Which tissue conducts water from the roots?
questions.explanation: Xylem conducts water and mineral ions through the plant.

topics.title: Photosynthesis
topics.description: How green plants use light energy to make glucose.

sections.heading: The process
sections.body: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants use light energy absorbed by chlorophyll to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water. Oxygen is released. Word equation: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen. The process stores some light energy as chemical energy in glucose.

sections.heading: Conditions and limiting factors
sections.body: Photosynthesis needs light, chlorophyll, carbon dioxide, and water. The rate can be limited by whichever needed factor is in shortest supply. Increasing light or carbon dioxide may increase the rate only until another factor becomes limiting. Glucose may be used in respiration, converted to starch for storage, or used to build other substances.

keyTerms.definition: A green pigment that absorbs light energy for photosynthesis.
A factor in shortest supply that restricts the rate of a process.
Iodine solution turns blue-black when starch is present.

questions.prompt: Which substances are used as raw materials in photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Plants use carbon dioxide and water to make glucose; oxygen is released as a product.

questions.prompt: What does chlorophyll do in photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll absorbs light energy that powers the production of glucose.

topics.title: Transport in plants
topics.description: Water movement, transpiration, and sugar transport.

sections.heading: Water and transpiration
sections.body: Water absorbed by roots travels through xylem to stems and leaves. Evaporation of water from leaf surfaces followed by diffusion of water vapour out through stomata is called transpiration. This water loss helps maintain an upward flow of water through the xylem. Wind, temperature, humidity, and light can affect the rate.

sections.heading: Transporting sugars
sections.body: Phloem transports dissolved sugars, especially sucrose, from sources such as photosynthesising leaves to sinks such as growing tissues and storage organs. Movement of dissolved products through phloem is called translocation. Unlike the xylem's main upward flow, phloem transport can occur in different directions in different sieve tubes.

keyTerms.definition: Loss of water vapour from a plant, mainly through leaf stomata.
Movement of dissolved organic substances through the phloem.
A source supplies a substance; a sink uses or stores it.

questions.prompt: Which tissue mainly carries water from roots to leaves?
questions.explanation: Water and mineral ions move through xylem tissue from roots towards stems and leaves.

options: Loss of water vapour from leaves
Movement of dissolved sugars through phloem
Movement of water through the soil
questions.explanation: Phloem translocates dissolved sugars from sources to parts of the plant that use or store them.

topics.title: Ecosystem basics
topics.description: Organisms, habitats, food chains, and energy flow.

sections.heading: Ecosystems
sections.body: A habitat is a place where an organism lives. A population is a group of organisms of one species in an area; a community is all the populations there. An ecosystem includes the community and the non-living environment, such as water, soil, light, and temperature, and their interactions.

sections.heading: Food chains and energy
sections.body: Producers, such as green plants, make organic food. Consumers obtain food by eating other organisms, while decomposers break down dead material and return nutrients to the environment. In a food-chain diagram, an arrow points from the organism eaten to the organism that eats it, showing the direction of energy transfer. Less energy is available at each higher trophic level.

keyTerms.definition: A community of organisms and the non-living environment with which they interact.
An organism that makes organic food, usually using photosynthesis.
An organism that breaks down dead organic material.

questions.prompt: Which organism is usually a producer in a terrestrial food chain?
questions.explanation: Green plants make organic food using photosynthesis and are producers.

questions.prompt: In grass → grasshopper → frog, what does the arrow from grass to grasshopper show?
questions.explanation: The arrow points from the food to the consumer and shows the direction in which energy is transferred.
